newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian reforms take backseat over snap poll fears.
newsitem.headline: Indian reforms take backseat over snap poll fears.

text.p: India's political parties, sensing potential for a snap election, have chosen class, religion and ethnic issues as the battleground for votes and left a slowing economy on the backseat, analysts said on Monday.

The parliament which ended its winter session on Friday, is due to reconvene for the crucial budget session in February. But most political parties were directing their energies elswehere, analysts said.
And speculation is mounting that Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's fragile coalition may not survive a power struggle within the Congress party, which supports the government from outside.

The main opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) said its immediate agenda was to install a government of its choice in the most populous state of Uttar Pradesh, a proven springboard for the BJP's recent successes.

The BJP, regarded as a Hindu upper caste party, is divided in Uttar Pradesh over its attitude to the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) of erstwhile Hindu untouchables, unsure whether to form its own government or to back the BSP in a three-corner tussle.
Prime Minister Gowda's United Front, with wide support among Moslems and low caste Hindus, is the third claimant to power in Uttar Pradesh.
"Deve Gowda's government has failed on all fronts and now it is engaged in subterfuge to stall the BJP. But he knows he cannot stop us for much longer," BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj told Reuters.
The state has been under Delhi's direct rule since a September poll there produced a hung assembly.
The state's High Court last week ruled a second consecutive extension of New Delhi's rule as invalid. The issue is now with the Supreme Court.
Deve Gowda's coalition, under fire from leading business clubs for a slowdown in economic reforms they blame on political instability, has also been hit by rumblings in the Congress party.
Congress president Sitaram Kesri has on several occasions threatened to review his ties with the United Front.
While Deve Gowda and Kesri have openly denied the prospects of a snap poll, both are jockeying for advantage.
Kesri became Congress president after former prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned the post in September following court summons in a cheating case.

Rao, who denies any wrongdoing in that and two other cases, was forced to quit last week as head of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP), triggering fresh elections for the post in which Kesri could be a candidate.
Kesri's immediate political agenda is not dissimilar to Deve Gowda's. Both want to woo Moslems and low caste Hindus and the poor.
Kesri has asked former Congress finance minister Manmohan Singh, architect of India's reforms, to "put a human face" on the party's economic agenda, implying an appeal to the poor.
He has also removed most upper caste leaders from Rao's days from the decision-making Congress Working Committee, replacing them with religious minorties and low caste Hindus.
"Nothing should be done to upset Mr Kesri's plans to bring back Moslems, Dalits and other minorities back to the Congress," former Congress minister Kamaluddin Ahmed said.

Deve Gowda, insisting that economic refroms cannot succeed unless they tackle the problem of poverty, told a Moslem convention on Sunday that India's largest minority community should not allow itself to be politically exploited.
Both Kesri and Deve Gowda have promised to consider job reservations for Moslems and low caste Hindus in the private sector, a suggestion frowned upon by industry.
